name: Tokyo
tagline: From the ten-seat shrine where Obama tasted the best sushi of his life to the solo ramen booth that went viral.

Sukiyabashi Jiro.description: Jiro Ono's sushi shrine, the "god of sushi" who inspired the documentary Jiro Dreams of Sushi. Barack Obama said it was the best sushi of his life.

Myojaku.description: Rose from two to three Michelin stars in 2026, with minimalist cuisine from chef Hidetoshi Nakamura in Nishi-Azabu.

Toriki.description: A neighborhood yakitori spot in Hatanodai that Anthony Bourdain called one of the best meals of his life. More than 35 years in business.

Tsukiji Outer Market.description: Tokyo's most famous street seafood market, with stalls for tuna, sea urchin, and sweet omelette since dawn.

Gogyo.description: Birthplace of black ramen (kogashi), with signature burnt garlic, in Nishi-Azabu.

Kanamachi Seimen.description: An orthodox neighborhood ramen shop in Katsushika, best paired with shochu or beer.

Sushi Saito.description: One of Tokyo's most exclusive sushi temples: chef Takashi Saito serves only a handful of diners a night in Roppongi, with a years-long waitlist. Three Michelin stars.

Sushi Yoshitake.description: Seasonal edomae-style sushi in Ginza from chef Masahiro Yoshitake, known for creative touches within tradition. Three Michelin stars.

Kyubey.description: Sushi house founded in 1935 in Ginza, one of Tokyo's oldest and most respected, long favored by dignitaries and international celebrities.

Sushi Dai.description: A former Tsukiji institution now inside the Toyosu Market, famous for its pre-dawn queues and market-fresh omakase sushi at relatively accessible prices.

Daiwa Sushi.description: Sushi Dai's historic rival inside Toyosu Market, with the same pre-dawn queue ritual for cuts fresh off the auction floor.

Sushi Zanmai Honten.description: The original Tsukiji flagship of the Kiyomura chain, open 24 hours and famous because its president has paid record sums for the year's first tuna at auction.

Uogashi Nihon-Ichi.description: A stand-and-eat sushi counter in Tsukiji, fast and affordable, made for grabbing a couple of pieces on your feet between market stalls.

Nihonryori RyuGin.description: Avant-garde kaiseki from chef Seiji Yamamoto in Roppongi, a regular on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list and holder of three Michelin stars.

Narisawa.description: Chef Yoshihiro Narisawa's 'satoyama' cuisine in Minami-Aoyama, a pioneer in blending French technique with Japanese forest ingredients. Two Michelin stars.

Den.description: Playful, irreverent kaiseki from chef Zaiyu Hasegawa, with signature dishes like the 'Dentucky Fried Chicken.' Two Michelin stars and a World's 50 Best regular.

Florilège.description: Chef Hiroyasu Kawate's chef-driven cuisine in Omotesando, blending French technique with Japanese produce at an open counter. Two Michelin stars.

Quintessence.description: Chef Shuzo Kishida's haute French cuisine in Shirokanedai, with a tasting menu built around seasonal produce. Three Michelin stars.

L'Effervescence.description: Chef Shinobu Namae's contemporary French cooking in Nishi-Azabu, strongly shaped by seasonal Japanese produce. Two Michelin stars.

Ginza Kojyu.description: Refined kaiseki from chef Toshiya Kadowaki in Ginza, prized for its seasonal precision. Three Michelin stars.

Kanda.description: Chef Hiroyuki Kanda's minimalist kaiseki in Azabu-Juban, one of the classic reference points of Japanese haute cuisine. Three Michelin stars.

Ishikawa.description: Seasonal kaiseki in a traditional house in Kagurazaka, led by chef Hideki Ishikawa. Three Michelin stars.

Sazenka.description: Chef-driven Chinese cuisine in Nishi-Azabu, one of the few Chinese restaurants in Tokyo with Michelin recognition for its reinterpretation of Sichuan and Cantonese classics.

Tempura Kondo.description: Chef Fumio Kondo's vegetable and seafood tempura in Ginza, famous for frying sweet potato until it's almost dessert-like. Two Michelin stars.

Tempura Mikawa.description: Classic edomae-style tempura in Fukagawa, with master Tetsuya Saotome a historic reference point for the craft. One Michelin star.

Nodaiwa.description: An eel (unagi) house founded in 1846 in Higashi-Azabu, grilling over charcoal with a recipe kept through generations.

Obana.description: A century-old eel restaurant near Senso-ji in Asakusa, known for its unadon served in a traditional Japanese house setting.

Sarashina Horii.description: A soba house founded in 1789 in Azabu-Juban, one of Tokyo's three great historic schools of buckwheat noodles.

Kanda Yabu Soba.description: A soba house open since 1880 in Awajicho, its interior garden and tatami room preserving a Meiji-era atmosphere.

Namiki Yabu Soba.description: Traditional soba since 1913 beside Asakusa's Senso-ji temple, with the dark, salty broth typical of old Edo-style noodles.

Ichiran.description: A tonkotsu ramen chain world-famous for its solo 'flavor concentration' booths, a format that went viral on social media and draws travelers from everywhere.

Afuri.description: Light yuzu-shio ramen born in Ebisu, a pioneer of a cleaner, citrus-forward style set against traditional pork-based ramen.

Fuunji.description: One of Shinjuku's benchmark tsukemen (dipping noodle) spots, with a thick dried-fish-and-chicken broth that draws constant queues.

Nakiryu.description: Spicy tantanmen ramen in Minami-Otsuka that became one of the first ramen shops in the world to earn a Michelin star.

Tsuta.description: At its original Sugamo location, Tsuta made history in 2016 as the first ramen restaurant in the world to earn a Michelin star.

Ippudo.description: The original Tokyo branch of the tonkotsu ramen chain founded in Fukuoka in 1985, which helped popularize Japanese ramen around the world.

Rokurinsha.description: Intensely flavored tsukemen on Tokyo Station's Ramen Street, one of the shops that drove the worldwide dipping-noodle craze.

Menya Musashi.description: Double-broth (fish and pork) ramen in Shinjuku, theatrically served and one of the most influential names in the scene since the 1990s.

Ramen Jiro (Mita Honten).description: The original 1968 shop of one of Japan's most cult-followed ramen chains, famous for colossal portions of pork, garlic and vegetables that spawned its own fandom ('Jirolians').

Kikanbo.description: Spicy ramen laced with karashi (Japanese mustard) and sansho pepper in Kanda, a distinctive style within Tokyo's ramen scene.

Bird Land.description: Upscale yakitori in a Ginza basement, chef Toshihiro Wada grilling select cuts of chicken over binchotan charcoal. One Michelin star.

Torishiki.description: Neighborhood yakitori in Ebisu recognized with Michelin's Bib Gourmand for excellent value.

Omoide Yokocho.description: A postwar Shinjuku alley packed with tiny yakitori and izakaya stalls shoulder to shoulder, visited by Anthony Bourdain in his Tokyo episodes.

Nonbei Yokocho.description: A postwar alley of tiny bars beside Shibuya station, nicknamed 'Drunkard's Alley'.

Andy's Shin Hinomoto.description: An izakaya tucked under the train tracks in Yurakucho, run for decades by a British fishmonger settled in Tokyo, hugely popular with both expats and locals.

Albatross.description: A tiny two-floor bar in Golden Gai, Shinjuku's postwar maze of 200-plus bars, decorated like a miniature Victorian parlor.

Bar High Five.description: A Ginza cocktail counter run by veteran bartender Hidetsugu Ueno, regarded as one of the world's best for his hand-carved ice technique.

Star Bar Ginza.description: One of Japan's most influential classic cocktail bars, a pioneer of the precision bartending school that defines Ginza.

Zoetrope.description: A Japanese whisky specialist bar in Shinjuku, stocking hundreds of rare labels and closed-distillery bottlings curated by its expert owner.

Maisen.description: Tokyo's flagship tonkatsu since 1965, housed in a former public bathhouse in Omotesando, famous for its crisp breaded pork cutlet.

Tonki.description: A neighborhood tonkatsu spot in Meguro since 1939, with an open kitchen and an atmosphere unchanged for decades; Anthony Bourdain visited it on No Reservations.

Butagumi.description: A Nishi-Azabu tonkatsu spot offering a menu of more than a dozen pig breeds from across Japan, upscale within its genre.

Jojoen.description: One of Japan's oldest and best-known yakiniku chains, founded in 1946, grilling wagyu cuts tableside.

CoCo Ichibanya.description: The world's largest Japanese curry chain, born in Nagoya in 1978, popular with travelers for letting diners customize spice level and toppings.

Delhi.description: Japanese-style curry in Ginza since 1956, one of Tokyo's most veteran curry houses with a loyal office-worker following.

Isetan Shinjuku Depachika.description: The basement food hall of Isetan department store in Shinjuku, considered Tokyo's most prestigious depachika, with dozens of stalls for fine pastry and gourmet bento.

Mitsukoshi Ginza Depachika.description: The food basement of Japan's oldest department store, with wagashi, seafood and delicatessen stalls in the heart of Ginza.

Takashimaya Nihonbashi Depachika.description: The food hall inside Nihonbashi's historic Takashimaya building, a designated cultural property, with a wide selection of high-end sweets and takeaway food.

Uobei Shibuya Dogenzaka.description: Fast-belt sushi in Shibuya where orders are placed by tablet and arrive on a bullet-train-style track straight to the table, a format that went viral on video.

Sushiro.description: Japan's largest kaiten (conveyor-belt) sushi chain, with plates starting at very low prices and digital ordering, popular with tourists and families alike.

Umegaoka Sushi no Midori (Shibuya).description: The Shibuya branch of an affordable sushi chain born in Umegaoka, famous for its enormous queues and value for money.

Café de l'Ambre.description: A coffee shop founded in 1948 in Ginza by a pioneer of Japanese coffee culture, still serving beans aged for years by its own methods.

Bear Pond Espresso.description: A specialty coffee shop in Shimokitazawa regarded as a pioneer of high-quality espresso in Tokyo, founded by barista Katsuyuki Tanaka.

Streamer Coffee Company.description: A Shibuya coffee shop founded by world latte-art champion Hiroshi Sawada, known for its foam designs and urban vibe.

% Arabica Nakameguro.description: The Nakameguro branch of the minimalist coffee chain that went viral on Instagram for its all-white aesthetic and views over the cherry-tree canal.

Pelican.description: An Asakusa bakery founded in 1942, famous for a simple, pillowy white loaf; Anthony Bourdain visited for its iconic toast.

Viron.description: A French bakery in Shibuya that imports flour from France for its baguette, considered among the best in Tokyo outside France itself.

Centre The Bakery.description: A Ginza cafe specializing in thick-cut toast from artisanal white loaves, offering different breads and jams on the side.

Toraya.description: A traditional Japanese sweets (wagashi) house with more than five centuries of history, a purveyor to the imperial family since the Muromachi era.

Higashiya Ginza.description: A contemporary wagashi house in Ginza, reinterpreting traditional Japanese confectionery with minimalist design.

Aragawa.description: One of Japan's most legendary and expensive steakhouses, open in Shinbashi since 1967, specializing in charcoal-grilled Tajima wagyu.

Ginza Steak.description: A hot-plate wagyu steak chain very popular with tourists for its value and its theatrical open-kitchen setup.

Sasa no Yuki.description: A tofu-kaiseki restaurant in Uguisudani tracing its recipe back to the Edo period, one of Tokyo's oldest tofu specialists.

Otafuku.description: An oden house founded in 1873 in Asakusa, one of Tokyo's most venerable spots for this winter stew.

Usukifugu Yamadaya.description: A pufferfish (fugu) specialist with several Tokyo branches, sourcing directly from Usuki in Oita, the birthplace of this culinary tradition.

Tsukishima Monja Street.description: A Tsukishima street lined with more than seventy monjayaki spots, okonomiyaki's runnier cousin cooked on a griddle and shared at the table.

Nakamise-dori.description: A centuries-old shopping street leading to Senso-ji temple in Asakusa, lined with stalls selling ningyo-yaki, senbei and other traditional sweets.

Toyosu Market.description: The wholesale market that succeeded Tsukiji in 2018 as Tokyo's largest fish auction hub, with tuna-auction viewing decks and attached sushi restaurants.

Gyukatsu Motomura.description: A specialist in gyukatsu (breaded beef cutlet served rare, to finish cooking yourself on a hot stone), a trend that went viral with tourists in Shibuya.

Torikizoku.description: A single-price izakaya chain founded in Osaka, hugely popular for cheap yakitori and drinks, with many branches across Tokyo.

Kanda Matsuya.description: A soba house from 1884 in Kanda, its traditional wooden building a recognized landmark with a loyal following across generations.

Jangara Ramen.description: Kyushu-style tonkotsu ramen in Harajuku since 1987, with a creamy pork broth and marinated egg, popular with the neighborhood's young crowd.

Tapas Molecular Bar.description: An intimate eight-seat counter at the Mandarin Oriental Tokyo, serving a molecular-gastronomy menu as a sequence of small chef-driven 'tapas'.

Ginza Sushiko Honten.description: An edomae sushi house founded in 1885 in Ginza, considered one of Tokyo's oldest and most prestigious, historically favored by political and business elites.

Shibuya Yokocho.description: A covered food alley opened in 2020 beside Shibuya station, with more than twenty stalls recreating the atmosphere of traditional yokocho, hugely popular on social media.

Ameyoko Market.description: A street market that emerged after World War II between Ueno and Okachimachi, with stalls of dried seafood, fruit and street food at bargain prices.

Kagari.description: Chicken paitan-broth ramen in Ginza, almost creamy in texture, with constant queues despite its discreet alley location.

Tsurutontan.description: An udon chain known for bowls so large they dwarf the diner's head, with locations open into the small hours in Roppongi and elsewhere.

Sometaro.description: An okonomiyaki house in a traditional Asakusa home, open since 1937, where diners cook their own griddle seated on the floor.

T.Y. Harbor.description: A restaurant and craft brewery beside the canal on Tennozu Isle, set in a converted warehouse, popular with Tokyo's international community.

Sushisho Masa.description: Upscale sushi in Roppongi from chef Masaaki Sasaki, trained in the Sushi Saito lineage, holding three Michelin stars.

Yoroniku.description: Upscale yakiniku in Ebisu, serving select wagyu cuts piece by piece in a sushi-counter style. One Michelin star.

Rengetei.description: A yoshoku (Western-influenced Japanese) restaurant founded in 1895 in Ueno, famous for its rice omelette (omuraisu), one of the style's pioneers in Japan.

Taimeiken.description: A yoshoku restaurant founded in 1931 in Nihonbashi, famous for its classic omuraisu and for its culinary reputation referenced in the film Tampopo (1985).

Kikunoi Tokyo.description: The Akasaka branch of Kyoto's legendary Kikunoi kaiseki house, led by chef Yoshihiro Murata, holding three Michelin stars.

Ukai-tei Ginza.description: Upscale teppanyaki in Ginza specializing in grilled wagyu and lobster, with an elegant setting popular with international visitors.

New York Grill.description: A restaurant on the 52nd floor of the Park Hyatt Tokyo, immortalized in the film Lost in Translation (2003), with panoramic city views and a famous Sunday brunch.

Shirube.description: A beloved neighborhood izakaya in Shimokitazawa, with an extensive menu of homestyle Japanese dishes and a lively, welcoming atmosphere.

Ebisu Yokocho.description: A former covered market converted into an alley of small izakaya stalls in Ebisu, a popular nighttime gathering spot.

Château Restaurant Joël Robuchon.description: A replica 18th-century French château in Ebisu Garden Place, the flagship Japanese outpost of chef Joël Robuchon, a longtime multi-star Michelin winner.
